figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Left: Accuracy of judging preferred or undesirable outputs on the validation set during training. Right: Reward margins between preferred and undesirable outputs on the validation set during training. More details about these experiments are given in the appendix.
figures.headline: Vanilla DPO models show low judgment accuracy and a reward margin that plateaus during training.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 2 (left), models using vanilla DPO perform poorly in distinguishing between preferred and undesirable outputs, failing to identify errors in rejected answers.

Additionally, Fig. 2 (right) shows that the reward margin (i.e., the gap between the rewards of preferred and undesirable outputs) is limited for models using vanilla DPO and plateaus with further training.
While DPO has proven effective in chat benchmarks, it brings only marginal improvements for long-chain reasoning tasks such as mathematical problems, as shown in Fig. 2 and Table 3.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Comparison between DPO and Step-DPO.
figures.headline: Diagram contrasts DPO comparisons of whole answers with Step-DPO comparisons of the first erroneous step.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Fig. 3, unlike vanilla DPO, which only considers preference optimization between complete answers (i.e., $p(y_{win}|x)$ and $p(y_{lose}|x)$), Step-DPO examines the step-by-step answer (i.e., $y=s_{1},...,s_{n}$) and specifically targets the first erroneous reasoning step.

As illustrated in Fig. 3, given a prompt $x$ and a series of initial correct reasoning steps $s_{1\sim k-1}=s_{1},\ldots,s_{k-1}$, Step-DPO aims to maximize the probability of the correct next reasoning step $s_{win}$ and minimize the probability of the incorrect one $s_{lose}$.

abstract: Mathematical reasoning presents a significant challenge for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to the extensive and precise chain of reasoning required for accuracy. Ensuring the correctness of each reasoning step is critical. To address this, we aim to enhance the robustness and factuality of LLMs by learning from human feedback. However, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has shown limited benefits for long-chain mathematical reasoning, as models employing DPO struggle to identify detailed errors in incorrect answers. This limitation stems from a lack of fine-grained process supervision. We propose a simple, effective, and data-efficient method called Step-DPO, which treats individual reasoning steps as units for preference optimization rather than evaluating answers holistically. Additionally, we have developed a data construction pipeline for Step-DPO, enabling the creation of a high-quality dataset containing 10K step-wise preference pairs. We also observe that in DPO, self-generated data is more effective than data generated by humans or GPT-4, due to the latter’s out-of-distribution nature. Our findings demonstrate that as few as 10K preference data pairs and fewer than 500 Step-DPO training steps can yield a nearly 3% gain in accuracy on MATH for models with over 70B parameters. Notably, Step-DPO, when applied to Qwen2-72B-Instruct, achieves scores of 70.8% and 94.0% on the test sets of MATH and GSM8K, respectively, surpassing a series of closed-source models, including GPT-4-1106, Claude-3-Opus, and Gemini-1.5-Pro. Our code, data, and models are available at https://github.com/dvlab-research/Step-DPO.

sections.body:
Vanilla DPO gives minimal benefit on long-chain mathematical reasoning. Per Fig. 2, models trained with vanilla DPO struggle to tell preferred outputs from undesirable ones, and their reward margin plateaus with further training.

Step-DPO instead treats each intermediate reasoning step as the unit of preference optimization and targets the first erroneous step. The paper describes a three-step pipeline (error collection, step localization, rectification) that builds about 10K step-wise preference pairs. It states that self-generated steps work better as preferred data than steps written by humans or GPT-4, as shown in Table 4.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Vanilla DPO cannot locate errors in long math reasoning, so Step-DPO compares individual reasoning steps instead.

sections.body:
This section reviews prior work in several directions: chain-of-thought prompting variants, supervised fine-tuning with data augmentation, external tools, continued pre-training, and reinforcement learning with step-by-step verification.

The authors state that these methods have not fully mitigated hallucinations, plateau once data reaches a certain volume, or still depend on reward model quality and complex RLHF pipelines. DPO is described as simpler and effective on chat benchmarks but offering only marginal benefit for mathematical reasoning. Step-DPO is positioned as a simpler, more efficient method that builds on DPO for long-chain reasoning.
sections.heading: Related Works
sections.headline: Prior methods improve math reasoning through prompting, data augmentation or reinforcement learning, but each has stated limits.

sections.body:
The step-wise formulation keeps the DPO objective but conditions on the prompt and the initial correct steps. It maximizes the probability of a correct next step and minimizes the probability of an incorrect one.

The data pipeline first collects wrong answers by prompting with a step-wise Chain-of-Thought prefix. It then finds the first erroneous step, and samples continuations from the reference model that reach the ground-truth answer. The first step of such a continuation becomes the preferred step. The authors state that these in-distribution steps are preferred over GPT-4 or human-rectified steps, which are out-of-distribution for the model. Manual or GPT-4 filtering is needed when a correct final answer contains flawed intermediate steps.
sections.heading: Step-DPO
sections.headline: Step-DPO builds preference pairs from the first wrong step, with the model's own correct continuation as the preferred choice.

sections.body:
Step-DPO is applied to open instruction models (DeepSeekMath-RL, Qwen2-72B-Instruct) after their prior RLHF training, and to supervised fine-tuned models trained on a 299K SFT dataset.

For Qwen2-72B-Instruct, Step-DPO reaches 70.8% on MATH and 94.0% on GSM8K. The text says this surpasses GPT-4-1106, Claude-3-Opus and Gemini-1.5-Pro. Models exceeding 70B parameters gain approximately a 3% boost on the MATH test set. Ablations show vanilla DPO gives limited benefit compared with Step-DPO, and in-distribution data outperforms GPT-4-corrected out-of-distribution data (Table 4). On competition-level problems, the text reports 50.1% on Odyssey-MATH for Qwen2-72B-Instruct.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Step-DPO raises Qwen2-72B-Instruct to 70.8% on MATH, with approximately a 3% boost for models above 70B.

sections.body:
The conclusion restates the method: Step-DPO uses a single reasoning step as the unit of preference comparison, which gives fine-grained process supervision and helps locate errors in incorrect answers.

It also restates the 10K-pair data construction pipeline and says the results show significant improvements, particularly for large models. The authors hope Step-DPO offers new insights into alignment for long-chain reasoning problems. The section does not add new experiments or report new numbers.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors conclude Step-DPO with 10K pairs gives significant gains, particularly for large models.
